title: Universal Basic Income: A Viable Socioeconomic Model?
content:
The concept of Universal Basic Income (UBI)—an unconditional, periodic cash payment delivered to all citizens on an individual basis, without means test or work requirement—has transitioned from a utopian fringe theory to the forefront of mainstream economic discourse. This resurgence in popularity is primarily driven by anxieties surrounding the imminent automation of millions of jobs via artificial intelligence and advanced robotics.

Advocates posit that UBI would eradicate extreme poverty, dismantle the stigma and bureaucratic inefficiency associated with traditional welfare systems, and provide individuals with the financial security to pursue education, entrepreneurial ventures, or caregiving roles. It essentially decoupling survival from traditional wage labor.

Detractors, however, raise formidable concerns regarding the macroeconomic feasibility of such a scheme. Funding a comprehensive UBI would likely necessitate exorbitant taxation levels, potentially stifling economic growth and disincentivizing workforce participation. Furthermore, critics argue that untargeted payments to the affluent are an inefficient use of public funds, and that UBI fails to address underlying structural issues such as the soaring costs of housing and healthcare. Pilot programs in various countries have yielded mixed results, leaving the debate far from settled.
